body: Ten minutes before the builders’ merchant opens — twenty past eight on a Thursday — a man of about forty-five is sitting in the cab of a flatbed outside it with two envelopes on the passenger seat, both from the same company, and he has opened one of them. The radio is on because it is always on, and a presenter with a very kind voice is talking about generosity in a season of plenty. He is not annoyed by this. He finishes a sausage roll, folds the bag into the door pocket, and at half past eight goes in to ask whether they will put another four hundred pounds on the account.

Nothing in that cab was a crisis of faith. It was smaller and more ordinary than that. The one institution in his life that talks about God was talking, that morning, on the one subject pressing on him, and it had nothing specific to say.

Money is one of the most heavily covered subjects in Scripture. It is in the law, all the way through the prophets, in most of the parables and in nearly every letter. Whatever else the text is shy about, it is not shy about this.

It is worth being specific about what is in there, because the range is far wider than the range of what gets said aloud. Wages are to be paid the same day, and the reason given is that the man is poor and counting on them. Interest taken from a brother is forbidden. Weights and measures are to be honest. The corners of a field are left unharvested, so the harvest itself is arranged around people who own nothing. Debts are released in the seventh year, and land goes back in the fiftieth to the family that lost it. That one is called the jubilee. This whole station family is named after a debt law.

The dial runs from HM 300.30 to HM 398.70 and carries 121 stations. One of them is given to this subject and to nothing else: HM 387.20, Money & Faith, assigned and in build and not yet on air, with a Steward’s Hour at eight in the morning and Generosity Stories at six in the evening already written into its published schedule.

Taking no money from listeners costs this band the most obvious way of paying for itself, and it is exactly why there is a frequency assigned to money with no audio on it yet. The teaching gets built when there is money to build it, and the money does not come from the people it teaches. That is a slow way to do it and it was chosen deliberately, because the alternative closes the subject before a word is spoken. A station funded by its listeners cannot teach freely about money. It has a position, and everyone can hear it.

It is worth saying plainly that the silence on those stations is not cowardice, and the people who keep them on air deserve better than to be sneered at from a distance. Christian radio has kept hymns going in towns that had nothing else, it runs on margins that would close a commercial operator inside a year, and its staff are paid less than they are worth by people who believe every word of the appeal they are making. The trouble is structural. Every sentence a listener-funded station says about money is heard against its own interest, the presenters know it, and so the subject gets handled at arm’s length.

This band is arranged so that teaching does not sit inside the music. The five-fold band carries the ministry stations, and the Bible-study frequencies hold their own numbers, together, in their own stretch of the dial. A subject can therefore be given a frequency rather than a slot, which means it never has to justify itself against the ratings of whatever it would otherwise be interrupting. It also means you can find it in the dark, and avoid it in the dark, and those turn out to be the same skill.
There are two things a station can do with money once it has decided to speak at all. It can appeal, or it can advise.

The budgeting-and-debt-freedom kind of Christian teaching took the subject seriously when very little else in the church would, and it has got real people out of real trouble. Anybody who has sat at a table with a couple and a carrier bag of unopened post knows what it is worth to hear somebody say: here is a plan, here is the order to pay things in, here is what to stop. What it cannot do is work the other way across the ledger. It addresses the listener as a spender, so it says almost nothing about the wage that listener pays somebody else, what he may charge, or the seventh year. The parts that cost the listener go missing.
A subject you cannot afford to teach is a subject you do not hold.

A man of fifty-two is at his kitchen table at half past ten on a Thursday night with a laptop open and his phone beside it, because the two figures do not agree. He has four men on the books. The invoice that was to clear on Tuesday has not, and what is in front of him is whether the four get paid on Friday or the tax office gets paid on Monday, because this week he cannot do both. He has been in church every week of his life and could talk for an hour about generosity. He shuts the laptop at eleven with none of it decided and goes up, leaving the landing light on for the dog.
He was not short of teaching. He was short of teaching on the thing in front of him — not an error anyone could name, but an absence, in a man who was always there.

The honest cost of this arrangement is that it is slow, and slowness is not a small thing when a frequency sits assigned and silent for years. A band that asked its listeners for money could build faster, and there are people who would give gladly and never once feel worked on. Refusing that means the frequency on this subject stays quiet while easier stations go up ahead of it. Nobody should pretend that is costless.

But the speed would have been bought with the position. Everything said afterwards about wages, debt, charging and the treatment of people who own nothing would arrive attached to an interest, and a listener would be right to hear it that way. The slowness is not a defect in the funding model. It is the funding model. It is the only thing that will make the eventual sentences worth listening to, and it is why the frequency is being held empty rather than filled cheaply.

So the gap between how much the text says about money and how little of it reaches the air is neither a mystery nor a failure of nerve. It is a consequence of who pays. Change who pays and the subject opens back up: debt, wages, inheritance, what is owed to somebody with nothing. None of that makes this band right about money. It means only that it can afford to be wrong in public, which is the condition of being useful at all.
All of which is an argument about arrangements, and arrangements stay theory until something is actually playing.

Four kinds of programming run on this dial, and it helps to know they are there before you start turning. Most of it is music — praise and worship, gospel, country, hymns and a great deal besides. There is teaching and prayer, where the Word is opened and prayed through rather than sung. There is family programming, which is simply safe to leave on in a room with children in it. And there are the international stations, hosted in their own languages rather than translated into them afterwards. The teaching frequencies sit together, including the one still waiting on this subject.

If you want somewhere to start today, start at HM 315.20, Corner Cipher. It is Christian rap out of Atlanta, Marcus Reed on the mic, trap and lyrical and soul-gospel, and he talks about the block he actually came from. That is where this article has been heading, because money is not an abstraction in that music. Rent is in it. What people did when there was no work is in it. It is one of the few places on any dial where the subject turns up at the height ordinary life has it, said by somebody raising nothing from you and with no reason to keep the tone comfortable. You will not like every track. It was never built to be liked evenly.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download and no card — open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest and press play, and it starts. It is deliberately built for inexpensive phones and thin connections, so it works on the hardware people actually have. If you want it nearer to hand, add the page to your home screen and it will open like anything else on it. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how the band learns which frequencies people are really reaching for — which is how the next one gets built.

Take that as an invitation rather than an offer. The argument here has been that you can tell a good deal about a voice by knowing what it needs from you, and the only way to test that is to listen to one that needs nothing. Put HM 315.20 on this afternoon while you are doing something else, and then leave it alone. Nobody will ask you for anything this week or next. When the frequency on money does open, you will already know what this dial sounds like with nothing to sell, and whether the teaching sounds like that too.
